blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU. YoloMT is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier performance among generative vision models in its class. Distilled from a 27B teacher by SFT and GRPO, it leads every model under 1B parameters on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench and Video-MME, answered from its captions, and beats LFM2.5-VL-1.6B and SmolVLM2-2.2B. YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and make them informative, encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens. This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes, making it efficient and effective. We also provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, with its stages and data, as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.

blocks.en:
While deep learning has enabled significant advancements in computer vision, offering new capabilities [ 25 , 51 , 19 , 50 ] ,
beyond traditional tasks like image classification and object detection, such as image captioning,
image generation and their video counterparts [ 67 , 52 , 84 , 27 ] , the deployment of these models in real-time settings with high-volume data
remains a challenge [ 70 , 43 , 31 ] . In particular, the need for generative outputs from live video streams, such as descriptions,
commentary, answers, and alerts, requires models that can operate efficiently on small GPUs at the edge [ 13 , 14 , 62 , 57 ] .
In order to operate effectively in these scenarios, a few constraints must be met, including the ability to process and generate outputs
in real time while maintaining high-quality performance without incurring significant computational costs [ 30 , 71 , 60 ] .
This has led to the development of smaller vision-language models (VLMs) that are designed for question answering on images or clips
under a budget constraint [ 15 , 44 , 66 , 6 , 55 ] .
In this work, we are particularly interested in making a sub-500M-parameter model that can scale with the number of frames it can read
efficiently and effectively, adjustable at run time for different scenarios and comparable to larger models on four
benchmarks curated for captioning and answered from the captions alone: OVO-Bench Real-Time [ 39 ] , MVBench [ 38 ] , StreamingBench Real-Time [ 40 ] , and Video-MME [ 21 ] .

blocks.en:
We formulate streaming captioning as one fresh description per second of a sliding recent window. Caption generation
is stateless: each caption reads the current frame and L L past frames sampled at one frame per second, without the previous caption
or language-model state. The visual cache persists, but generated text does not. A fixed-size cache and bounded
per-frame work keep memory bounded and latency predictable, while L L remains adjustable at run time. But overlapping
windows also produce overlapping descriptions: persistent facts recur even without copying the previous caption.
For a rolling state log, each caption can update the current state rather than append another report of the same
event. In video surveillance and anomaly detection, an alert monitor can read the descriptions continuously and
merge repeated alerts for the same event. These consumers must treat overlap as repeated coverage, not independent
evidence. We evaluate the captions, not a complete monitoring system.

blocks.en:
YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and infer from them without additional vision passes. It also sets the quality–cost
frontier among generative vision models in its class, and we provide a detailed recipe for training it that we think could be useful for other
tasks as well, along with ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.
Our model is distilled from a larger teacher model and trained using a combination of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement
learning. We observe that the model learns to understand the temporal context of the video stream and to generate high-quality captions.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU,
YoloMT, which is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier
performance among generative vision models in its class ( Fig. 4 ). 2. We introduce an architecture that reads more frames cheaply and makes them informative,
encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens ( You Only Look Multiple Times: YoloMT, a Real-Time Streaming Model on a T4 ).
This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes,
making it efficient and effective. 3. We provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, including its stages and data,
as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.

blocks.en:
Traditional computer vision tasks, such as image classification and object detection, have been significantly advanced by deep learning
techniques. The generative AI paradigm has expanded the scope of computer vision to include new tasks such as image captioning and
image generation, but this expansion came at the cost of an explosion in model size and computational requirements [ 33 , 54 , 43 ] , creating a split
between large generalist models, including proprietary ones, and smaller models that are more efficient but less capable [ 47 , 64 , 11 ] .
This split has shaped the field of small vision-language models (VLMs) [ 31 , 60 ] , which are designed for image and video
understanding [ 6 , 44 , 83 ] but are often limited in their ability to generate high-quality outputs in real-time scenarios [ 40 , 39 , 72 ] .
The main challenge has thus become how to design and train small VLMs that can operate efficiently in real-time settings
while maintaining the high-quality performance of larger models [ 55 , 16 , 63 ] .
Mobile-VideoGPT addresses this through lightweight dual visual encoders, frame selection and visual-token pruning [ 55 ] .
Other approaches optimize the architecture and training of small VLMs [ 66 , 82 ] , or change how much
visual information the language model reads. Matryoshka Multimodal Models and the Matryoshka Query Transformer train
one model to represent an image with different numbers of visual tokens at inference [ 10 , 29 ] .
This allows a trade-off between spatial detail and computation. In our setting, the adjustable budget instead controls
how many past moments the model reads, with a fixed number of tokens for each cached frame.

blocks.en:
The streaming setting adds another requirement: the model must generate outputs as new frames arrive, rather than
after receiving a complete clip. VideoLLM-online introduces a streaming training objective and inference pipeline for
conversation within a continuous video stream [ 13 ] . LiveCC trains on speech transcripts interleaved
with video frames and learns real-time commentary [ 14 ] . We study the same need for continuous generative
outputs, but focus on a fresh caption of the recent past every second, within the memory and per-frame time budgets
of a T4.

blocks.en:
Keeping the past available has led to several forms of streaming memory. Flash-VStream combines a compact temporal
context memory with a larger memory for retrieving spatial detail [ 81 ] . TimeChat-Online drops visual
tokens that do not change between frames [ 74 ] , while ReKV stores video key-value caches and retrieves
those relevant to a question [ 18 ] . Our model instead caches pooled visual tokens before the language model,
and does not carry the language model’s state from one caption to the next. Each sampled frame is encoded once and kept as 16 tokens in a ring
of recent frames. A caption reads the current frame and a chosen number of cached past frames, without another vision
pass. This is a bounded recent history for continuous captioning, rather than a memory for retrieving events from an
entire long video.

The distinction is where state lives, rather than whether memory is bounded. StreamingVLM also bounds its KV cache,
but carries attention sinks, recent visual tokens and a longer text history [ 71 ] . Our captions
instead restart from the selected visual window. Each caption is thus independent of earlier outputs, and L L can
change from one caption to the next, but nothing enforces novelty across overlapping captions. Text is also an interface for anomaly detection: LAVAD captions frames, then
uses an LLM to aggregate descriptions over time and estimate anomaly scores [ 78 ] . Such aggregation belongs
to the downstream consumer.
Socratic Models and LLoVi answer video questions from captions [ 79 , 80 ] ; VDCscore [ 12 ] and CaptionQA [ 73 ] score captions by the answers they support. We bring this to streaming, where
captions precede the questions.

blocks.en:
More history is not always more useful. SimpleStream shows that a recent-frame window can match more elaborate
streaming models, and that adding history can weaken current-scene perception [ 58 ] . SelectStream
addresses this by exposing history through a compact, query-conditioned evidence budget while keeping the current
frame visible [ 23 ] . These findings motivate both parts of our approach: making past frames
cheap to read, and training the model to infer from them. Our controls separate the information in those frames from
the tokens and computation used to read them ( Sec. 4.1 ).

blocks.en:
Previous work has also explored distillation techniques that transfer knowledge from larger models to smaller
ones [ 26 , 34 , 9 , 2 , 11 ] . We use this to specialize a small model for captioning,
first through the teacher’s captions and then through reinforcement learning. To serve different lookbacks with one
set of weights, we apply the sandwich rule of slimmable networks [ 76 , 75 ] to the number of past
frames rather than network width. Our work brings these architectural and training choices together in a streaming
model that runs within the budget of a T4, and measures what the main choices contribute. While we focus on streaming captioning, we
believe the recipe could also be useful for other generative vision tasks [ 13 , 14 , 22 , 61 ] .

blocks.en: 3.1 Architecture: look once, read many
blocks.zh: 3.1 建筑:一看,多读

blocks.en:
YoloMT employs the architecture of LFM2.5-VL-450M [ 6 ] , with a vision encoder and a language model, and adds a
pooler ( Fig. 2 a). The vision encoder, SigLIP2 [ 65 ] , processes each frame once, and the pooler caches
its representation as 16 tokens, allowing the model to read multiple past frames without re-encoding them. The language
model, LFM2.5-350M [ 6 ] , generates captions based on the current frame and the cached representations of past
frames. The idea is to allow the model to look at past frames without incurring the computational cost of re-encoding
them, enabling efficient streaming captioning in real time.
The number of cached frames that the model reads, 16 visual tokens each, is referred to as the lookback L L ,
which can be adjusted at run time to the amount of past context the model should consider when generating captions. The
input prompt to the language model consists of a template, the cached blocks of past frames, and the tokens of the
current frame. The model is trained to generate captions of 30–50 words that describe the last 16 seconds of video; the
previous caption is not part of the prompt.

At deployment, we spread the work of a caption across the incoming frames of the 30 FPS stream ( Fig. 5 ).
The first frame of each second runs the vision encoder and the pooler. Each following frame processes one chunk of at

pass or a longer chunk of work per frame. The deployment budget is 16 ms of GPU work per incoming frame, under 2 GB
of memory, and a completed caption before the next second. We provide the architecture and engine details in the
supplementary material ( Secs. A.1 and A.3 ).

The training of YoloMT is based on classical distillation techniques, where a larger teacher model is
used to provide supervision for the smaller student model. The training process consists of three stages.

In the final stage, we use reinforcement learning to further improve
the quality of the captions generated by the student model. We use the GRPO [ 56 ] algorithm, where we sample
64 windows per step and generate eight captions for each window at one shared lookback L L .
We choose the largest available L L with probability 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} , otherwise uniformly from zero through that maximum.
For each distinct valid caption among the 512 rollouts, Qwen3.5-9B is queried online. It extracts atomic facts
and checks each against the union of the teacher’s claims for precision. In the other direction, it checks whether the
caption states or implies each consensus claim for recall. The same judge answers the window’s multiple-choice
questions from the caption alone and rates its fluency; a frozen small language model provides a separate fluency score.
We batch these text-only requests, with duplicate captions of a window scored once per step ( Sec. B.1 ).
The advantage is computed as A i = ( R i − R ¯ ) / σ R A_{i}=(R_{i}-\bar{R})/\sigma_{R} within the group, and groups with equal rewards are dropped
as in [ 77 ] . The update is the PPO-clipped surrogate [ 53 ] , averaged over the tokens of the step
with clip 0.2, and a per-token KL penalty with coefficient β = 0.04 \beta{=}0.04 pulls towards the frozen SFT model
( Sec. B.2 ). Without it the model drifts towards repeating certain phrases and producing fact-free closers
( Sec. 4.1 ). The training stops after
three evaluation checks without gain (phi-4 [ 1 ] scores greedy dev captions every 50 steps), and a
tripwire is used to tighten the reward when the training reward rises but the evaluation score does not. The reward is
defined as: R = g ⁡ ( λ 1 ​ recall + λ 2 ​ precision + λ 3 ​ mcq ) + λ 4 ​ fluency , R=g\,(\lambda_{1}\,\mathrm{recall}+\lambda_{2}\,\mathrm{precision}+\lambda_{3}\,\mathrm{mcq})+\lambda_{4}\,\mathrm{fluency}, (3) where λ 1 = 0.4 \lambda_{1}=0.4 , λ 2 = 0.3 \lambda_{2}=0.3 , λ 3 = 0.2 \lambda_{3}=0.2 and λ 4 = 0.1 \lambda_{4}=0.1 weight the four terms.
The gate g ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] g\in[0,1] scales the factual terms using the judge’s fluency rating and a repetition penalty.
The additive fluency term instead rewards likelihood under the frozen language model; both are normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ( Sec. B.1 ). A caption over 60 words receives R = 0 R=0 for the whole sum, including the additive fluency term.

blocks.en:
We evaluate YoloMT on four public benchmarks with questions built from human annotations:
OVO-Bench [ 39 ] , StreamingBench [ 40 ] , Video-MME [ 21 ] and
MVBench [ 38 ] .
We curate these benchmarks for streaming captioning by keeping only the parts that captions of the last 16
frames can answer: we leave out questions that need audio, memory far beyond 16 s, dialogue state or a
decision of when to speak ( Sec. C.1 ).
Each model captions the videos as a live stream, from a fixed prompt and blind to the question, and a text-only
answerer 2 2 2 Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, temperature 0, one option letter. answers from the captions
alone. This setup, new for streaming captioners, separates what a model sees from how it reasons: one answerer
serves every model, so accuracy measures what the captions carry, and every answer can be inspected against the
captions behind it.
The captioning model is run at 1 FPS and 256 × \times 256 resolution, reading L = min ⁡ ( t , 16 ) L{=}\min(t,16) past frames at
the question’s last second t t .
For each baseline, we select among the same three fixed prompts: plain description, live narration and concrete facts.
The wording with the best mean phi-4 fact-F1 at L = 0 L{=}0 and 16 on 100 separate pilot windows wins.
These windows enter no reported result. We freeze the wording before any scored captioning, benchmarks included;
YoloMT keeps its training prompt ( Sec. C.2 ). This gives each baseline a choice rather than imposing
one wording on every model.
We also score the captions themselves by fact-F1 on held-out captions from LLaVA-Video test and OpenVid, unseen in
training but from the same distribution.
The fact-F1 score measures the recall of the teacher’s consensus claims and the precision of the caption’s atomic facts,
as judged by phi-4 [ 1 ] , and is reported as a percentage of the teacher’s agreement with itself. On these sets, Tab. 1 reports fact-F1 without a word-limit penalty, with the original 60-word-rule scores in parentheses
where they differ. That cutoff was a training constraint for YoloMT, but the baselines were only prompted for
30–50 words. Table 1 provides the main results of our evaluation, showing that YoloMT outperforms the other models
in its class on all four benchmarks, and is comparable to models several times its size.
On the mean of the four benchmarks, YoloMT leads LFM2.5-VL-450M by +5.0  [+3.7, +6.4 ] points, SmolVLM2-500M by +4.9  [+3.6, +6.2 ], Mobile-VideoGPT-0.5B by +8.2  [+6.8, +9.6 ] and FastVLM-0.5B by +3.3  [+2.0, +4.6 ]; on held-out LLaVA-Video test captions at L = 16 L{=}16 , it reaches
71.8 % of the teacher ceiling, against 46.7 % and 44.5 % for the first two.
Without the length penalty, InternVL3.5-2B leads YoloMT on test (78.3 % against
71.8 %), as the Qwen3-VL models and TimeChat-Online-7B (74.3 %) do; under the rule,
InternVL3.5-2B scores 59.3 %.
Among larger models, YoloMT leads LFM2.5-VL-1.6B by +3.5 [+2.1, +4.9 ]
and SmolVLM2-2.2B by +1.7 [+0.4, +3.0 ], as well as Qwen2.5-VL-7B and
LiveCC-7B, which write shorter captions; InternVL3.5-1B and InternVL3.5-2B lead it by +3.0 and
+5.7 points, and the Qwen3-VL models by +4.8 to +6.8. The streaming
models StreamingVLM-7B and TimeChat-Online-7B lead it by +1.5 [+0.1,
+3.0 ] and +4.2 [+2.8, +5.5 ] points.
YoloMT also runs in real time on a single T4: with frames run back to back, its TensorRT engine keeps the p99 time
per frame at 12.66–12.69  ms at every L L , within the 16 ms we allow per frame at 30 FPS,
with 1.05  GB of memory ( Fig. 5 ). With arrivals paced at 30 FPS, the p99 is
14.3–15.0  ms, still within the same budget. At an equal 45 tokens per caption in the same TensorRT engine,
YoloMT shows its caption within 0.50  s at L = 16 L{=}16 , against 0.93  s for
LFM2.5-VL-450M; SmolVLM2-500M finishes no 45-token caption within its second at L ≥ 8 L\geq 8 ( Sec. A.3 ).
Even in eager PyTorch, YoloMT is the fastest model we timed: it writes a 50-token caption in 1.13  s at L = 16 L{=}16 , against 1.35  s for LFM2.5-VL-450M and up to
8.17  s for the others, and the 7B and 8B models do not fit on a T4 at all. Quantized
to INT4 and served with vLLM, Qwen3-VL-2B writes a caption in 0.84  s, but with
5.24  GB of memory, over the 2 GB budget.
We also show the performance of every model against its time per caption, memory usage and size
( Fig. 4 ).
We also evaluate the effect of reading more past frames on different models on the four benchmarks,
and show that not only can YoloMT read more past frames without significant computational cost,
but reading more past frames also improves its accuracy ( Sec. D.1 ): from L = 0 L{=}0 to 16, its mean
accuracy rises by +2.5 [+1.2, +3.7 ] points, while its 50-token caption takes
no longer (1.17 and 1.13  s). This is not a property that its base model, LFM2.5-VL-450M, has by default: it loses
accuracy with more past frames ( − - 1.7 [ − - 3.0, − - 0.4 ], Sec. D.1 ). We attribute
this to the temporal context that YoloMT learns to use through its training.
On held-out videos, we can directly observe how the captions generated by YoloMT evolve
with additional temporal context ( You Only Look Multiple Times: YoloMT, a Real-Time Streaming Model on a T4 ). The examples in Sec. D.4 show how the past changes
what the captions describe: with the past, YoloMT describes a water lily opening and the camera moving around a parked car;
without it, the captions describe the flowers and the car largely as still scenes. The past supplies the change in
the scene or the viewpoint, rather than just more details of the current frame.

The first claim we check is the central claim of the paper: for a strong captioning model,
reading more past frames is important, which is why making it cheap is the key to a strong model ( Sec. D.2 ).
We first check whether compute explains the gain in performance: we provide the current frame 16 times

real past.
We then check whether the model is reading the past frames: we provide the past frames of a different video.
The model then scores 18.7 %, far below no past frames at all (52.7 %), which confirms that the model
is indeed reading the past frames and inferring from them. The gain therefore comes from the evidence in those
frames, not just from a longer prompt.
We end these controls by checking the temporal order, keeping the same past frames. Shuffling them costs

facts a caption states, not the order of the events, so this control cannot show whether the model reads frame order.

blocks.en: 5 Discussion and limitations
blocks.zh: 5. 讨论和限制

blocks.en:
Nothing in the architecture or in the recipe is specific to captioning: the cached
frames, the lookback chosen at run time, the per-frame schedule, SFT over many lookbacks and GRPO with a shared lookback
and a KL penalty would apply as they are to other generative tasks on video streams, such as answering questions or
raising alerts. A new task enters the recipe only through the teacher’s labels and the reward. We have, however, run the
recipe once: on streaming captioning, with one student family and a horizon of 16 s.
On its own view, the teacher scores 122.3 % of the ceiling at L = 16 L{=}16 on dev, and YoloMT 72.2 %. Our ablations point to the student’s capacity as a limit on its performance
( Sec. 4.1 ): a larger student trained on the same labels scores far higher, and YoloMT misses recall and
precision about equally (0.505 against 0.841, 0.580 against
0.887). More data helped only with more training, so we expect the gap to close with the capacity of
the student rather than with more labels, which is the trade-off we make by staying under 500M parameters.

blocks.en:
While the recipe is general, we have run it on only one task, with one model architecture as the student.
The gap to the teacher’s performance is hypothesized to be due to the student’s capacity; whether the size
of the student or its architecture is the limiting factor is unknown.
The teacher model, Qwen3.8-27B, while performant in our tests, is still far from the state of the art
in vision capabilities, and whether a student model can be further improved by a teacher with higher-quality
outputs is left to future work.
We have also read the benchmarks through captions, keeping the parts that captions can answer. This setup shows
what each model’s captions carry, but it scores general-purpose models on the task ours was
trained for, a limitation that labels covering more general vision tasks could address.

blocks.en: LLM Usage Statement
blocks.zh: LLM 语言 用法声明

blocks.en:
We used large language models in three ways. First, as components of the method: a 27B vision-language model wrote
the training labels, a 9B model extracted facts and scored the rewards, a 14B model judged the held-out captions, and a
24B model answered the benchmark questions from the captions ( Secs. 3.2 and 4 ). Second, as coding
agents: Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) wrote code for training, evaluation, deployment and the
figure and table scripts, and launched and monitored experiments; the authors audited the code. Third, for this paper:
the same agents searched the literature through the arXiv API, built the reference list from arXiv records, checked
the numbers in the text against the result files, drafted parts of the text and corrected grammar and typos. The
authors wrote most of the text, revised every passage, and verified every cited paper.

blocks.en:
YoloMT reads one fixed prompt in training and at inference. Its text never changes: the slot of the previous caption always
reads “none” ( Sec. A.1 ). The L L pooled blocks follow, oldest first, then the 64 tokens of the present; the
listing writes L L as K.

The protocol is the same for FastVLM-0.5B, StreamingVLM-7B and TimeChat-Online-7B:
the L + 1 L{+}1 frames in one request, the selected wording, greedy decoding and at most 80 new tokens. The two streaming
models therefore do not run in their own interaction format. TimeChat-Online-7B keeps its token drop, which removes every
visual token whose cosine similarity to the token at the same position one frame pair earlier exceeds 0.5; it keeps
51 % of its visual tokens at the protocol L L , and all of them at L = 0 L{=}0 , where no earlier pair exists.
StreamingVLM-7B, trained to comment on a stream turn by turn, answers such a request with its silent token. We therefore
ban its silent tokens, require at least one token and apply its own repetition penalty. Its captions then start as a
description and repeat themselves until the token limit (67 words on average on the benchmarks); on
the held-out sets, the 60-word rule scores most of them 0 ( Tab. 1 ). Its numbers measure this adaptation, not its own
streaming commentary.

blocks.en:
Fact-F1 uses three sets of windows, disjoint by source video from each other and from the training data. The LLaVA-Video
dev split has 1,103 windows of 42 videos, LLaVA-Video test 1,518 windows of 56 videos, and
held-out OpenVid 1,008 windows of 466 clips from 405 videos. These are the windows with a
ceiling. A window has none when the derivation of its claims did not complete, when its consensus is empty or when none of
its questions survived; this leaves out 354, 530 and 244 windows with 16 stored
past seconds. Dev and test windows are consecutive seconds of the same episodes, a median of 27 windows per
video. 522 of the 526 windows that select the RL checkpoint ( Sec. B.1 ) are dev windows, the
other 4 have no ceiling, and the remaining 581 dev windows select nothing. Dev therefore serves curves, ablations and controls, while the comparisons
with the baselines use the held-out sets and the benchmarks. The 100 prompt-pilot windows of Sec. C.2 come from dev videos but have no ceiling, so they are in none of these sets.

blocks.en:
The score of one caption on one window comes first. The judge splits the caption into atomic facts and checks them
against the teacher’s claims of the window, with the prompts of Sec. E : recall is the share of the
consensus claims that the caption states or clearly implies, precision the share of the caption’s facts that the
union states or clearly implies, and raw fact-F1 their harmonic mean, from 0 to 1. The target is the consensus of all
kept teacher samples and the union of every teacher caption of the window. The original scoring protocol then gives 0
to a caption over 60 words, the 60-word rule: Tab. 1 reports held-out scores without it and gives the rule’s
scores in parentheses where they differ, while the dev results, as in Sec. 4.1 , and Tabs. S8 and S9 keep it. Only checkpoint selection multiplies raw fact-F1 by the gate g g of Sec. B.1 , as gated fact-F1, and only Tab. S8 reports raw fact-F1, since the pilot
windows have no ceiling. Everywhere else, fact-F1 is a share of the teacher ceiling: a model’s raw fact-F1 summed over
the windows of a set, divided by the ceiling’s sum over the same windows. The ceiling of a window is the raw fact-F1 of
one teacher caption, the first of the window’s samples at temperature 0.7, against a target built without
it: the claims of at least 5 of the other 7 kept samples (the same fraction, rounded up,
when fewer are kept) and the union of every other caption, the greedy one included. Every judging run scores the
ceiling again. The ceiling is therefore the teacher’s agreement with itself, not an upper bound: 100% means agreeing
with the target as well as one teacher sample agrees with the others, not recovering every visible fact. The teacher’s
greedy caption meets a union that holds the claims of its own stored label, so it exceeds the ceiling, as on dev at L = 16 L{=}16 ( Fig. S1 a).

blocks.en:
Repeating the current frame keeps the prompt and its length but removes the gain from history, and another video’s
past falls far below no past at all, so the gain comes from what the past frames show ( Tab. S11 ).
Shuffling the real past costs much less; fact-F1 ignores the order of events, so this control does not test it. A
consensus of 16 samples [ 69 ] , at 16 times the decoding, recovers at most 7 % of the
real past’s gain. Blending cached seconds into extra blocks at test time gains nothing: the cache is not read at a
finer grain than it was trained on.
